about.dates: This report covers your session on Tuesday 20 October 2026 and was prepared on 20 October 2026. If a session is re-analysed, the report is prepared again and carries the new date.
about.footnote: Measured and prepared with PinPoint Studio. Video stays in the studio.
about.measured: 10 swings with a 7 iron, filmed down-the-line and face-on at high frame rate, with every ball measured by a GC Quad. Your body positions are read from the video by pose tracking; the club and ball numbers come from the launch monitor.
about.notChecked: Some things could not be checked on every swing. How fast the club was moving at its peak: our cameras could see it, but not well enough to judge (10 of 10 swings). When your hips turned fastest: the face-on camera cannot time a turn while you are square to it; a down-the-line camera or a body sensor can (7 of 10 swings). When your chest turned fastest: the face-on camera cannot time a turn while you are square to it; a down-the-line camera or a body sensor can (3 of 10 swings). Where that touches one of your work-ons, its page says so.
about.ranges: Each habit is judged against a target range. Most ranges are coaching judgement, set from what good ball-strikers do; a few come from published measurements. They are not fitted to you. A swing outside the range is not a mistake in itself — it is where the evidence points. “Ruled out” on a work-on page means measured, and fine, on these swings with these cameras — not gone for good.

rows.name: Pelvis moves toward the ball in the backswing

causes.lead: We couldn't pin down what drives this one today. Here are the possible causes: the ones we couldn't check, and the ones we've ruled out.

items:
A quick physical test would tell: Turning your hips without your chest · Lead-hip mobility
Hidden on today's swings: Your shoulders start down before your hips
rows.title: Could be behind it — we couldn't check

items: Your hips are slow to start turning coming down
rows.title: Ruled out — measured, and fine

workOns.check: Film face-on and step through the start of the downswing. Your belt buckle should start turning toward the target while your back is still facing it.
workOns.cue: From the top, feel your weight press into your lead foot and your belt buckle start to turn before your shoulders join in.

drills.instruction: Start with your feet together, make a backswing, and step toward the target with the lead foot as you start down. Small shots first.
drills.label: Step-through
drills.note: It exaggerates on purpose. The aim is the sequence, not the step.
drills.targets: To feel the weight arriving on the lead side before the club does.

drills.instruction: Make swings with a one-second pause at the top. From the pause, start down with your lower body, letting your weight move toward your lead foot while your chest stays behind the ball for a moment. Start with half swings and short irons.
drills.label: Pause at the top
drills.note: The pause is a rehearsal, not a new swing. Once the order feels natural, let the pause shrink until it has gone.
drills.targets: To give your lower body time to start the downswing, so your upper body is not rushed toward the ball.

workOns.goal: Let your hips lead and your shoulders follow
workOns.kicker: Work-on 1 of 5  ·  P7, at impact  ·  3 of 3 swings
workOns.name: Out-of-order sequence
workOns.saw: Your body turns in the wrong order coming down — on all 3 swings. Typical when your hips reached full speed: at impact. It could not be measured on 7 of 10 swings: the face-on camera cannot time a turn while you are square to it; a down-the-line camera or a body sensor can.
workOns.why: When your chest or arms peak before your hips, your body stops adding speed and your arms are left to make it.

workOns.cameWith: The coaching model says it can bring other habits with it. Not today — on every swing we could see, you strike the ball cleanly, without catching it on the edge and you get the ball up in the air.

causes.lead: One possible cause showed up on the same swings. Because both happened on every swing, we can't prove one drives the other — so here is what we spotted, what we couldn't check and what we've ruled out.

items: You stand up through the ball — on 10 of 10 swings
rows.title: What we spotted

items: A quick physical test would tell: Core stability · Upper-back mobility · Lead-hip mobility
rows.title: Could be behind it — we couldn't check

items: You stand up out of your posture going back
Your posture at address is hard to swing from
rows.title: Ruled out — measured, and fine

workOns.check: Film from down the line. At impact your back and hips should still sit on the lines you drew at address.
workOns.coachTerm: Coaches call the habit Loss of posture, or “loss of posture”, “losing your posture”.
workOns.cue: Feel your chest stay over the ball and your seat stay back until the ball has gone.

drills.equipment: a wall, or the back of a chair
drills.instruction: Stand with your back to a wall and set up so that your backside just touches it, with a club held across your chest. Turn slowly to the top and back down to where impact would be. Your trail back pocket should stay on the wall going back, and your lead back pocket should find it as you turn through, without pushing hard into it or coming away from it.
drills.label: Backside on the wall
drills.note: If your hips can only turn by moving toward the ball, the limit may be in how far your hips can turn, and a physical check comes before more practice.
drills.targets: To feel your hips turn while keeping their distance from the ball, so your arms keep the room they had at address.

drills.instruction: Hold an alignment stick along your spine, touching the back of your head, your upper back and your tailbone. Rehearse your address position and your backswing turn keeping all three in contact.
drills.label: Rod along the spine
drills.note: A fixed upper-back curve will stop all three touching. That is information, not a failure.
drills.targets: To feel the spine angle you set at address being kept through the turn.

workOns.goal: Keep your address posture through the ball
workOns.kicker: Work-on 2 of 5  ·  P7, at impact  ·  10 of 10 swings
workOns.name: Loss of posture
workOns.saw: You stand up out of your posture through impact — on all 10 swings, no change from first swing to last.
workOns.why: Standing up lifts the bottom of your swing, so contact gets thin and harder to repeat.

workOns.cameWith: The coaching model says it can bring other habits with it. Not today — on every swing, your head stays level going back, your hips hold their height going back and you keep your posture going back.

rows.title: Could be behind it — we couldn't check

items: You squat too much at address
rows.title: Ruled out — measured, and fine

workOns.check: Film from down the line. At the top, your trail knee should look about as bent as it did at address.
workOns.coachTerm: Coaches call the habit Trail knee straightens, or “standing up on it going back”.
workOns.cue: As you turn back, feel your trail knee stay soft and pointing at the ball while your trail pocket turns behind you.

drills.equipment: an alignment stick outside the trail hip, optional
drills.instruction: Take your address position, make a slow backswing turn, and stop at the top. Feel the pressure in the trail hip socket rather than on the outside of the trail foot. Hold for three seconds, then return.
drills.label: Trail hip load and hold
drills.note: The stick is a feedback aid, not the drill. If the hip cannot rotate internally, the slide is the body finding the only route it has.
drills.targets: To feel the trail hip accepting the turn instead of the pelvis sliding away from the target.

workOns.figureLabel: Each dot is one swing: trail-knee bend lost by the top, in degrees.
workOns.goal: Keep the flex in your trail knee
workOns.kicker: Work-on 3 of 5  ·  P4, at the top  ·  10 of 10 swings
workOns.name: Trail knee straightens
workOns.saw: Your trail leg straightens going back — on all 10 swings, no change from first swing to last. Typical trail-knee bend lost by the top: 22°, against a target of 12° or less; this is a clear miss: well past the range on 9 of 10 swings.
workOns.target: Trail-knee bend lost by the top: 12° or less, on most swings. Today: 22°.
workOns.why: A straight trail leg lets your hips slide instead of turn, so you lose power.

workOns.cameWith: The coaching model says it can bring other habits with it. Not today — on every swing, your trail shoulder works down and under into impact.

rows.title: Could be behind it — we couldn't check

items: Your hips are slow to start turning coming down
You hang back on your trail side through impact
rows.title: Ruled out — measured, and fine

workOns.check: Film face on. At impact you should see the front of your lead hip, with your belt buckle turned toward the target.
workOns.coachTerm: Coaches call the habit Hips under-rotated at impact, or “hips not clearing”, “blocked”.
workOns.cue: Through the ball, feel your belt buckle already facing between the ball and the target.

drills.equipment: a mirror or a phone on a stand
drills.instruction: Make slow swings to impact and stop there. Check three things: your belt buckle points between the ball and the target, your trail heel is just off the ground, and your hands are level with your lead thigh with the shaft leaning a little toward the target. Hold for two seconds, then finish the swing slowly.
drills.label: Impact hold
drills.note: A held position is not a swing: use it to learn what impact feels like, then hit gentle shots trying to pass through it. If your hips will not open without your shoulders opening too, that is a mobility question before it is a practice one.
drills.targets: To feel where your body and hands need to be when the club reaches the ball.

drills.instruction: Make slow half swings and keep your chest and belt buckle turning after the ball until both face the target. Stop with the club at waist height, your arms in front of your chest and the back of your lead hand facing the target. Hold for a second, then go again.
drills.label: Turn to the target
drills.note: If your hips will not turn through without your lead knee buckling or your lower back complaining, have your lead hip checked before repeating this one.
drills.targets: To feel the body carrying the club through the ball, so the hands have no need to take over.

workOns.figureLabel: Each dot is one swing: hip turn at impact, in degrees.
workOns.goal: Turn your hips partly open by impact
workOns.kicker: Work-on 4 of 5  ·  P7, at impact  ·  10 of 10 swings
workOns.name: Hips under-rotated at impact
workOns.saw: Your hips haven't turned enough by impact — on all 10 swings, no change from first swing to last. Typical hip turn at impact: 3°, against a target of 18° or more; this is a clear miss: well past the range on all 10 swings.
workOns.target: Hip turn at impact: 18° or more, on most swings. Today: 3°.
workOns.why: Hips that haven't turned enough get in your arms' way, so your hands take over and the strike varies.

workOns.cameWith: It came with you stand up through the ball (10 of the 10 swings we could see). That fits the coaching model, though showing up together is not proof that one causes the other. And on every swing, the club travels along the target line through impact, the club comes into the ball at the right angle for the club in your hands and your strikes stay near the middle of the face.

workOns.check: Film from down the line. Coming down, your hands should drop below the line they went up on, never out above it.
workOns.coachTerm: Coaches call the habit Over the top, or “coming over it”, “OTT”.

consistency.basisText: σ 1.5% hand rise · 0.34 of corridor · n 10

workOns.cue: Start down by letting your trail elbow drop toward your trail hip pocket, as if your hands were falling straight down.

drills.instruction: Place two tees, or a headcover just outside the ball, so the club has to travel through a gate to reach it. Start with slow half swings.
drills.label: Gate drill
drills.note: Set the gate for the path you want, not against the one you have — a gate that punishes the current swing without offering another produces a flinch, not a change.
drills.targets: To feel the club approaching from a different direction, with immediate feedback when it does not.

drills.instruction: Swing to the top, then move down to about waist height and stop, checking that the shaft is on the plane it started on and your hands still have their angle. Return to the top and repeat three times, then hit the shot.
drills.label: Pump to delivery
drills.note: Rehearsal, not a swing thought. Trying to do this consciously at full speed produces a different, slower swing.
drills.targets: To rehearse the delivery position rather than to arrive at it by accident.

workOns.figureLabel: Each dot is one swing: hands coming down outside the way they went up, in percent hand rise.
workOns.goal: Bring your hands down inside the path they went up
workOns.kicker: Work-on 5 of 5  ·  P4, at the top  ·  10 of 10 swings
workOns.name: Over the top
workOns.saw: Your hands come over the top coming down — on all 10 swings, no change from first swing to last. Typical hands coming down outside the way they went up: 12% hand rise, against a target of 8.7% hand rise or less; this is mostly a small miss, but well past the range on 3 of 10 swings.
workOns.target: Hands coming down outside the way they went up: 8.7% hand rise or less, on most swings. Today: 12% hand rise.
workOns.why: When the club comes over the top it cuts across the ball, so you tend to pull it or slice it.
